thread.title: Facebook’s Election Vow To Muzzle ‘Bad Actors, Misinformation’

author: Jon Swartz
title: Facebook’s Election Vow To Muzzle ‘Bad Actors, Misinformation’
text:
By Jon Swartz July 24, 2018 6:55 p.m. ET Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg Illustration: Bloomberg News The View From Silicon Valley
Like a crusading politician, Facebook (FB) has made an election vow: It is determined to significantly reduce the influence of bad actors and misinformation in the U.S. midterms and other elections globally this year.
But in an hour-long briefing with reporters late today that laid out a litany of preventive measures it is taking to avoid a repeat of the 2016 presidential election, it dodged questions on whether it has detected specific attacks, especially from Russia.
"We know there will be an attempt," Nathaniel Gleicher, director of Facebook's cyber security policy, said tersely.
Facebook has been under particular pressure to staunch the spread of misinformation after reports it allowed Russian-backed agents to buy ads and manage Facebook pages with the intent to stoke conflict on issues such as gun control and influence American voters.
Russia’s Internet Research Agency has proved an especially elusive target amid reports it is stepping up efforts to mask its activity.
On Wednesday, Facebook dismantled a right-wing fake news network ahead of elections in Brazil in October. Facebook deactivated 196 pages and 87 accounts of a network run by senior organizers from the Movimento Brazil Livre , or "Free Brazil Movement," according to a Reuters report.
The social networking giant was forthright in outlining measures it took in the Mexican general election on July 1, including the elimination of bogus profiles posing as politicians, debates broadcast via Facebook Live, and voter registration and information via the massive Facebook platform.
In particular, it trumpeted coordinated efforts of manual investigations team led by people, combined with automated detection and removal of fake accounts through machine learning and artificial intelligence, to restore election integrity. It claims to delete more than 1 million fake accounts per day before they can be reside on Facebook.
It's a Sisyphean undertaking. Facebook is trying to strike a "hard balance" of the expression of ideas on its platform with the safety of its community of 2.2 billion monthly active users, according to Tessa Lyons, product manager of News Feed. Indeed, Chief Security Officer Alex Stamos is leaving after voicing frustration over the company's missteps.
"We need to deprioritize short-term growth and revenue and to explain to Wall Street why that is OK," Stamos said in a memo obtained by BuzzFeed News . "We need to be willing to pick sides when there are clear moral or humanitarian issues. And we need to be open, honest and transparent about our challenges and what we are doing to fix them."
Feeling pressures from angry lawmakers in the U.S. and Europe, company Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has taken steps to clean up the platform by beefing up its security ranks to 20,000 by year's end, tweaking News Feed to minimize the influence of outside meddlers, rating the accuracy of news reports, and clearly identifying the buyers of political ads.
The fallout has been more political than financial, as evidenced by Facebook's record-setting stock price the past few weeks. On Tuesday, it closed at $214.67. That's up 22% so far this year.
The company hosted a meeting May 23 at its Menlo Park, Calif., headquarters attended by representatives from Amazon (AMZN), Apple (AAPL), Alphabet's Google (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), Verizon Communications (VZ) division Oath , Snap (SNAP), and Twitter (TWTR), according to two people with knowledge of the summit. They were not authorized to speak on the record.
The group of eight companies met with Christopher Krebs , an under-secretary for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) , and a representative of the FBI's newly formed "foreign influence" task force.
But critics like Jonathon Morgan , founder of the non-profit Data For Democracy , call the moves "cosmetic" and are convinced the 2018 midterm elections will be as vulnerable to social engineering and hacking as the 2016 presidential election. He claims multiple countries, including operatives from each side of the political spectrum in the U.S., have designs on influencing the midterms through comments, ads, and cyberintrusions.
"Social media just serves up things you think you are going to be interested in, it's hard to tamp down fake news," Vince Steckler , Chief Executive of security company Avast Software , tells Barron's . "You just need to influence a small group of voters to swing an election, as it happened in 2016."
Whether Facebook suffers financially from another election intrusion is another matter. The stock is up 30% over the last 12 months, and the company has a market value of $610.7 billion, despite its well-documented issues. The company is expected to announce strong second-quarter earnings on Wednesday.
How strong? Facebook has reported revenue above consensus the last 12 quarters, exceeding expectations by an average of 4%--$250 million to $300 million--according to a note from Goldman Sachs analyst Heather Bellini on Monday.
